pll1d8c2-d1e3477.summary: States that God's essence alone is properly called unchangeable, because it neither changes nor can change.
claims: Only God's essence is unchangeable in the proper sense.

pll1d8c2-d1e3480.summary: With De Trinitate V: other substances receive accidents and so change, but nothing can happen to God, so he alone is unchangeable, to whom being most truly belongs. What changes does not keep its being; what can change can cease to be what it was. So only what cannot change at all most truly is, namely the substance of Father, Son, and Spirit.
claims: Other substances receive accidents by which they change.
No accident can befall God.
What can change can cease to be what it was.
Being most truly belongs to what cannot change.

pll1d8c2-d1e3500.summary: Explains 1 Tim 6:16 ('who alone has immortality') with Augustine: since the soul is in some sense immortal, Paul's 'alone' means that true immortality is immutability, which no creature has.
claims: True immortality is immutability.
No creature has true immortality.

pll1d8c2-d1e3539.summary: Adds James 1:17: with God there is no change or shadow of alteration.
claims: God has no change or alteration.

pll1d8c2-d1e3554.summary: Adds Ps 101:28: you will change them and they will be changed, but you are the same.
claims: God remains the same while creation changes.

pll1d8c2-d1e3569.summary: With Augustine on Genesis: God moves neither in place nor in time, while creatures move in both; moving in time is being changed in affections. God says 'I am God and I do not change' (Mal 3:6), so he alone has immortality.
claims: God moves neither through place nor through time.
Creatures move through time and place.
Motion through time is change of affection.

pll1d8c2-d1e3593.summary: With Augustine against Maximinus: in every changeable nature, change is a kind of death, for it makes something not be what it was. So the immortal soul dies to justice or to sin, and heavenly creatures could die because they could sin. Angels sinned, and the impeccability of any rational creature is by grace, not nature; God alone by nature cannot change or sin.
claims: Every change is a kind of death.
The soul can die to justice or to sin.
Angels could and some did sin.
A rational creature's inability to sin is due to grace, not nature.
God alone by nature cannot change or sin.

pll1d8c2-d1e3625.summary: With De Trinitate I: we must try to behold the substance of God, which makes changeable things without change in itself and creates temporal things without temporal motion, difficult as that is.
claims: God makes changeable things without changing.
God creates temporal things without temporal motion.

pll1d8c2-d1e3645.summary: Concludes that only the essence of the Godhead is truly and properly unchangeable, having created all natures without change in itself.
claims: Only the divine essence is truly unchangeable.
God created all natures without change in himself.

pl-l1d8c2.summary: Treats divine immutability: God's essence alone is properly unchangeable, neither changing nor able to change, since it receives no accidents (Augustine). That is why only God 'has immortality' (1 Tim 6:16): true immortality is immutability, which no creature has by nature. Every changeable nature undergoes a kind of death, as the soul dies to justice or to sin and angels could sin; impeccability in creatures is by grace, not nature. God moves neither in place nor in time and creates temporal things without temporal motion.
claims: God's essence alone is properly unchangeable.
God can receive no accidents and so cannot change.
What can change, even if it does not, can cease to be what it was; so only the unchangeable most truly is.
True immortality is immutability, which belongs to the Creator alone.
Every change is a kind of death.
The human soul and angels are mutable and can sin; any rational creature's impeccability is by grace, not nature.
God makes changeable things without change in himself.
